paragraphs.title: Bildad’s Opening Claim About Divine Justice

easy.explanation: Job 8:1 begins, “Then answered Bildad the Shuhite.”
Bildad asks whether God or the Almighty would pervert judgment or justice.
easy.q: What does Bildad defend in his speech?

answers: Seek God and make supplication to Him
easy.explanation: Bildad tells Job to seek God and make his supplication to the Almighty.
easy.q: What does Bildad urge Job to do?

medium.explanation: Bildad says that if Job’s children sinned, God cast them away for their transgression.
medium.q: According to Bildad, why were Job’s children cast away?

answers: God would help him and prosper his dwelling
He would have to leave his land
medium.explanation: Bildad says God would awake for Job and make the habitation of his righteousness prosperous.
medium.q: What would happen if Job were pure and upright?

answers: Job’s beginning was limited, but his latter end would increase
medium.explanation: Bildad promises that Job’s latter end should greatly increase.
medium.q: What does “thy beginning was small” mean in context?

answers: Uprightness leads, in his view, to God’s help and prosperity
Uprightness prevents a person from seeking God
Uprightness makes a person depend on other people
challenge.explanation: Bildad connects being pure and upright with God’s intervention and future prosperity.
challenge.q: What connection does Bildad make between uprightness and a person’s condition?

answers: God does not pervert judgment or justice
God has no connection with judgment
challenge.explanation: Bildad asks, “Doth God pervert judgment?” and presents God as just.
challenge.q: What is Bildad’s main claim about God’s judgment?

answers: He speaks sharply but promises a better future if Job is upright
He praises Job but says there is no hope
He ignores Job’s condition and discusses only the past
challenge.explanation: Bildad rebukes Job while promising restoration and growth if Job is pure and upright.
challenge.q: How do Bildad’s words combine rebuke with hope?

answers: The former age and their fathers
easy.explanation: Bildad says, “enquire, I pray thee, of the former age.”
easy.q: Whom does Bildad tell Job to ask for instruction?

easy.explanation: He says human days are like a shadow upon the earth.
easy.q: How does Bildad describe human life?

answers: Teach and utter words from their heart
easy.explanation: Bildad says the fathers can teach, tell, and utter words from their heart.
easy.q: What can the fathers do, according to Bildad?

answers: Human life is brief, so earlier wisdom is valuable
There is no need to consider the present
medium.explanation: Because human days are brief, Bildad points Job toward the experience and teaching of the fathers.
medium.q: Why does Bildad direct Job to earlier generations?

answers: An earlier generation or ancient time
medium.explanation: “Former age” refers to the generations and times that came before.
medium.q: What does “former age” mean in this passage?

answers: Both emphasize the briefness of life and the value of inherited wisdom
Both describe the power of the wicked
medium.explanation: A shadow is temporary, so Bildad uses life’s brevity as a reason to learn from earlier generations.
medium.q: What idea is shared by “our days upon earth are a shadow” and Bildad’s reference to the fathers?

answers: The ability to teach from their experience
The ability to change God’s judgment
The ability to lengthen human life
challenge.explanation: Bildad presents the fathers as sources who can teach and speak from experience.
challenge.q: What authority does Bildad give to earlier generations?

answers: The wisdom of the past should be examined
Questions should no longer be asked
challenge.explanation: His command calls for careful inquiry into what earlier generations taught.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from Bildad’s command to search the fathers?

answers: Since life is brief, people should learn from those who lived before them
Since life is brief, learning is pointless
Since life is brief, the fathers’ words have no meaning
challenge.explanation: The shortness of life makes the wisdom of earlier generations especially useful.
challenge.q: How does the description of human life support Bildad’s advice?

paragraphs.title: The Plant That Depends on Water

easy.explanation: Bildad asks whether the rush can grow without mire and the flag without water.
easy.q: What plant examples does Bildad use?

easy.explanation: The plant withers when it lacks the water and mire it needs.
easy.q: What happens to the plant without water?

answers: It gains the wisdom of the fathers
easy.explanation: Job 8:13 says, “the hypocrite’s hope shall perish.”
easy.q: What happens to the hypocrite’s hope?

answers: As the plant needs water, those who forget God lose their hope
As the plant grows without water, those who forget God prosper
The plant and those who forget God are unrelated
medium.explanation: The plant’s dependence on water illustrates the loss of hope among those who forget God.
medium.q: What comparison does Bildad make between the plant and those who forget God?

answers: Wet mud or a marshy place
medium.explanation: Mire is wet, muddy ground in which the rush can grow.
medium.q: What does “mire” mean in this passage?

answers: It lacks the water and mire needed for growth
medium.explanation: The rush and flag cannot continue growing without their needed water source.
medium.q: Why does the plant wither quickly?

answers: Hope needs a sustaining source and perishes when that source is absent
Hope always survives regardless of circumstances
Hope depends only on outward appearance
challenge.explanation: The plant represents hope that cannot survive without a source of nourishment.
challenge.q: What does the plant illustration teach about the foundation of hope?

answers: A plant depends on conditions for life and can wither
A stone needs more water than a plant
challenge.explanation: Growth and withering make the plant a useful picture of dependence and loss.
challenge.q: Why is a plant a fitting comparison for those who forget God?

challenge.explanation: Bildad concludes that the path of those who forget God leads to the perishing of hope.
challenge.q: What result does Bildad present for those who forget God?

paragraphs.title: A Fragile Support and the Plant’s Fate

easy.explanation: Bildad says, “whose trust shall be a spider’s web.”
easy.q: What is the wicked person’s trust compared to?

easy.explanation: The passage says, “He shall lean upon his house, but it shall not stand.”
easy.q: What happens when the wicked person leans on his house?

answers: It is destroyed from its place
easy.explanation: If the plant is destroyed from its place, it is denied and no longer recognized.
easy.q: What eventually happens to the plant described in this passage?

answers: It looks like support but cannot hold him securely
It is made of strong stones
It provides water for the plant
medium.explanation: A spider’s web appears to be a structure, but it is too fragile to support someone.
medium.q: Why is a spider’s web a fitting picture of the wicked person’s trust?

answers: Its roots cling among stones but do not have secure permanence
The plant built its own house
The plant is surrounded by abundant water
medium.explanation: The roots appear to hold among the stones, yet the plant can still be removed.
medium.q: What does the plant’s roots being wrapped around a heap suggest?

answers: It is green and flourishing, but can later be destroyed and forgotten
It changes from dry to permanently flowering
It changes from a spider’s web into a tree
medium.explanation: The plant is first green and growing, but its place can later deny it.
medium.q: How does the plant’s condition change through the passage?

answers: It appears green, but it may be destroyed and forgotten
It appears dry, but becomes a house
It appears weak, but becomes a stone
challenge.explanation: The passage contrasts temporary greenness with the possibility of removal and loss.
challenge.q: What is the main contrast between the plant’s appearance and its fate?

challenge.explanation: The phrase presents the apparent joy or success of the plant’s way before the final outcome.
challenge.q: In context, what does “the joy of his way” most naturally suggest?

answers: They appear to provide support but are not secure
They possess strength that never changes
challenge.explanation: Both images portray something that seems supportive but cannot endure.
challenge.q: What idea is shared by the spider’s web and the plant’s insecure roots?

paragraphs.title: The Promise of God’s Help to the Righteous

easy.explanation: Bildad says, “God will not cast away a perfect man.”
easy.q: Whom will God not cast away?

easy.explanation: Bildad says God will fill Job’s mouth with laughing.
easy.q: What will eventually fill Job’s mouth?

answers: They will be clothed with shame
They will be clothed with joy
easy.explanation: The passage says, “They that hate thee shall be clothed with shame.”
easy.q: What will happen to those who hate Job?

answers: God will help him and restore his joy
He will remain in trouble forever
He will depend on the wicked’s house
medium.explanation: Bildad says God will not cast away the perfect man and promises Job laughing and rejoicing.
medium.q: What does Bildad promise the righteous person?

medium.explanation: The phrase refers to people who practice evil or wrongdoing.
medium.q: What does “evil doers” mean in this passage?

medium.explanation: Bildad concludes that the dwelling place of the wicked shall come to nought.
medium.q: What will happen to the dwelling place of the wicked?

answers: The righteous receive joy, while the wicked lose their dwelling
Both receive exactly the same outcome
The wicked rejoice while the righteous are shamed
challenge.explanation: The righteous are associated with laughing and rejoicing, while the wicked’s dwelling comes to nothing.
challenge.q: How does the passage contrast the righteous and the wicked?

answers: That Job is truly perfect or upright
That Job trusts in a spider’s web
challenge.explanation: The promise is connected to Bildad’s statement that God will not cast away a perfect man.
challenge.q: What condition is implied in Bildad’s promise of joy to Job?

answers: A mouth filled with laughing and lips with rejoicing
A house supported by a spider’s web
challenge.explanation: The images of laughing and rejoicing depict a dramatic movement toward restored happiness.
challenge.q: Which image most strongly emphasizes Job’s future change?
